genZNote: Nature's own genetic engineer — it naturally inserts its own DNA into plant cells to give itself a tumor to live in, and biotech just hijacked that trick to make GMOs.

morphology.notes: Carries the tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid, which contains T-DNA that is naturally transferred into and integrated into a host plant's genome.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, and wound sites on dicot plants
habitat.hostAssociation: Plant pathogen infecting a broad range of dicotyledonous plants; not associated with humans or animals
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Common soil bacterium worldwide; enters plants through wounds near the soil line

culture.media: Yeast extract-mannitol agar or nutrient agar
culture.colonyMorphology: Circular, convex, translucent to white, often mucoid colonies

identificationClues: Causes crown gall disease — tumor-like growths at plant wound sites, especially near the soil line
Virulent strains carry the Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid, whose T-DNA segment is transferred into and stably integrated into the plant genome
This natural trans-kingdom DNA transfer mechanism is repurposed in the laboratory as the standard method for creating genetically modified plants
Not a human or animal pathogen — its clinical/economic relevance is entirely agricultural and biotechnological

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Ti plasmid-mediated T-DNA transfer into plant genome
examFacts.importantDisease: Crown gall disease in dicot plants
examFacts.importantTest: Detection of the Ti plasmid in virulent isolates
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Natural genetic engineer of plants; its Ti plasmid system is the workhorse tool for making transgenic plants
